teach.title: Words that point
teach.say: To say *this* one or *that* one, Latin uses **the pointing words hic ('this'), ille ('that'), is ('that / the one we mean')**, *prōnōmina dēmōnstrātīva*. *Hic* points at what is near or has just been said, *ille* at what is further off, *is* at the one already known: *hic ānulus* = this ring, *illa taberna* = that shop, *is servus* = that slave, the one we mean.

teach.title: It dresses like its noun
teach.say: A pointing word stands beside its noun and matches it in gender, number and case, exactly as an adjective does. In the nominative (the subject form) that gives *hic ānulus* (masculine), *haec gemma* (feminine), *hoc ōrnāmentum* (neuter) and, for more than one, *hī puerī*. Choose the form from the noun, never from the English.

teach.title: When the noun is the object
teach.say: If the noun is what the verb acts on, the pointing word goes into the accusative (the object form) with it: masculine **hunc**, feminine **hanc**, neuter **hoc** — *hunc ānulum emit*, *hanc margarītam aspicit*. The object forms change more than you expect, so learn *hunc* and *hanc* as words in their own right rather than trying to reach them from *hic* and *haec*.

teach.title: The odd pair: huius and huic
teach.say: Two cells break the adjective pattern, and they are the same for all three genders. The genitive (the owner form) is **huius** — *pretium huius ānulī*, the price of this ring. The dative (the receiver form) is **huic** — *huic servō nummōs dat*, he gives this slave coins. One form each, learned as a pair.

teach.title: ille and is: the four cells to learn
teach.say: *Ille* and *is* take the same two odd cells: the genitive (the owner form) **illīus** and **eius**, the dative (the receiver form) **illī** and **eī**, one form each for every gender. Two more cells are not what you would guess either — the first form is *ille, illa, illud* and *is, ea, id*, never *illus* or *ius*, so a neuter thing is **illud** or **id** and never *illum* or *eum*. Everything else does follow an ordinary *-us -a -um* word: *illum*, *illō*, *eum*, *eō*, and *hōc* from *hic*.

teach.title: Pointing word, or linking word?
teach.say: English *that* does two jobs, and Latin keeps them apart. *That shop* points: *illa taberna*. *The shop that Lydia loves* links a clause to the noun: *taberna quam Lȳdia amat*. If you could say *which* or *who* instead, it is a form of *quī*; if you could say *this*, it is *hic* or *ille*. In *ille servus quī saccum portat* both are at work in one sentence.

core.text: To say *this* one or *that* one, Latin uses **the pointing words hic ('this'), ille ('that'), is ('that / the one we mean')**, *prōnōmina dēmōnstrātīva*. *Hic* points at what is near or was just mentioned, *ille* at what is far off, *is* at the one already known: *hic ānulus* = this ring, *illa taberna* = that shop, *is servus* = that slave (the one we spoke of).
*This / these* is close, *that / those* is far; often the distance is in the story, not in space. English has no word for the neutral *is*: use *that* or *the*.
hic haec hoc = this; ille illa illud = that; is ea id = the one meant. All three share an odd genitive in -ius (eius, huius, illīus) and one dative form for every gender (eī, huic, illī).

invented.la: Hic puer bonus est, ille puer improbus.
invented.en: This boy is good, that boy naughty.

core.text: English *that* does two jobs. *That shop* points: *illa taberna*. *The shop that Albinus has* links a clause: *taberna quam Albīnus habet* — the relative pronoun quī, quae, quod ('who, which, that'). If *that* could be *which* or *who*, it is *quī*; if it could be *this*, it is *ille* or *hic*.

more.text: From the learner's notes (week 8): a demonstrative stands with a noun and matches it in gender, number and case; the near demonstrative *hic, haec, hoc*, the far *ille, illa, illud*, and *is, ea, id* as distance-neutral, 'the one you know about' (*Id oppidum Bethlehem est*). All five demonstratives — *hic*, *ille*, *is*, *iste*, *ipse* — follow the -ius / -ī pattern of *alius*: genitive singular -ius and dative singular -ī for every gender, neuter singular sometimes -ud instead of -um. *Ille* follows it cleanly (*ille*, *illud*, *illīus*, *illī*). *Is* has an odd nominative (*is*, *id*) and a stem that switches between e- and i- (*eum*, *eius*, *eī*; plural *iī*, *eōrum*, *iīs* or *eīs*). *Hic* hides the pattern under a leftover -c from an old *-ce*: *hunc*, *hanc*, *huius*, *huic*, *hōc*, *hāc*.

Ørberg cap. VIII sets *is* and *ille* beside the question words: *is / ille servus*, *eum / illum*, *eius / illīus*, *eī / illī*, *eō / illō*; plural *iī / illī*, *eōs / illōs*, *eōrum / illōrum*. *Iste* is 'that of yours'; *ipse* is 'himself, the very one' (*lupus ipse*, r09:54.2). Neuter plural *haec* alone = these things. A&G §146, §296–298.
